units.title: Chapter B1: You and your genes

topics.title: B1.1 What is the genome and what does it do?

outcomes.text: Explain how the nucleus and genetic material of eukaryotic cells, and plasmids of prokaryotes, relate to cell function.
Describe how to use a light microscope to observe plant and animal cells.
Describe the genome as the entire genetic material of an organism.
Describe DNA as a polymer of nucleotides in a double helix.
Describe how the genome and environment together shape the phenotype.
Explain chromosome, gene, allele, variant, genotype and phenotype.
Explain how amino acids are polymerised into proteins under instructions from the genome.
Describe DNA nucleotides: a sugar and phosphate with one of four bases (separate science).
Explain how base sequence codes for proteins, three nucleotides per amino acid (separate science).
Recall a simple description of protein synthesis involving mRNA and ribosomes (separate science).
Recall that all genetic variants arise from mutations (separate science).
Describe how variants in coding DNA alter protein activity and phenotype (separate science).
Describe how variants in non-coding DNA alter gene expression and phenotype (separate science).

topics.title: B1.2 How is genetic information inherited?

outcomes.text: Explain gamete, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant and recessive.
Explain single gene inheritance, including genetic diagrams.
Predict the results of single gene crosses.
Use direct proportions and simple ratios in genetic crosses.
Use probability to predict the outcome of genetic crosses.
Recall that most features result from multiple genes.
Describe the development of genetics, including Mendel and genome sequencing (separate science).
Describe sex determination in humans.

topics.title: B1.3 How can and should gene technology be used?

outcomes.text: Discuss the importance for medicine of understanding the human genome, including disease alleles and genetic testing for family planning and healthcare.
Describe genetic engineering as modifying an organism's genome to introduce desirable characteristics.
Describe the main steps of genetic engineering: isolating the gene, putting it in a vector such as a plasmid, inserting it in cells and selecting modified cells.
Explain the benefits and risks, practical and ethical, of gene technology in agriculture and medicine.

topics.title: B2.1 What are the causes of disease?

outcomes.text: Describe the relationship between health and disease.
Describe communicable and non-communicable diseases.
Explain how communicable diseases from viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi spread in animals and plants.
Describe influenza, Salmonella, athlete's foot, malaria and sexually transmitted infections including HIV/AIDS.
Describe the plant diseases tobacco mosaic virus, ash dieback and crown gall.

topics.title: B2.2 How do organisms protect themselves against pathogens?

outcomes.text: Describe non-specific human defences: physical, chemical and microbial.
Explain how platelets are adapted to their function.
Explain the role of the immune system in defence.
Explain how white blood cells are adapted: ingesting pathogens, antibodies, antigens and memory cells.
Describe physical plant defences, including the leaf cuticle and cell wall (separate science).
Describe chemical plant defences such as antimicrobial substances (separate science).

topics.title: B2.3 How can we prevent the spread of infections?

outcomes.text: Explain how the spread of communicable diseases is reduced in animals and plants, including a human infection, a plant disease and STIs such as HIV/AIDS.
Explain how vaccines prevent disease, using safe forms of pathogens, and why a large share of the population must be vaccinated.

topics.title: B2.4 How can we identify the cause of an infection? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Describe ways of detecting and identifying disease, including plant disease, in the lab and field.
Describe how to use a light microscope to observe microorganisms.
Explain the aseptic techniques used in culturing organisms.
Calculate cross-sectional areas of cultures and clear zones around antibiotic discs using pi r^2.
Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced.
Describe how monoclonal antibodies are used in diagnostic tests.

topics.title: B2.5 How can lifestyle, genes and the environment affect health?

outcomes.text: Describe how genetic and lifestyle factors increase or decrease the risk of non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and type 2 diabetes.
Describe how to investigate the effect of exercise on pulse and recovery rate.
Use data to explain the incidence of non-communicable diseases locally, nationally and globally in terms of exercise, diet, alcohol and smoking.
Translate between graphical and numerical forms and construct frequency tables, bar charts and histograms.
Understand sampling and use scatter diagrams to identify correlation.
Describe interactions between different types of disease.

topics.title: B2.6 How can we treat disease?

outcomes.text: Explain the use of medicines, including antibiotics, in treating disease.
Calculate cross-sectional areas of bacterial cultures and clear zones using pi r^2.
Evaluate treatments for cardiovascular disease: lifestyle changes, medicines and surgery.
Describe discovery and development of new medicines, including preclinical and clinical testing.
Describe how monoclonal antibodies treat cancer, including tagging cells and delivering radioactive or toxic substances (separate science).

units.title: Chapter B3: Living together - food and ecosystems

topics.title: B3.1 What happens during photosynthesis?

outcomes.text: Describe photosynthesis, its two stages, the need for light and its endothermic nature.
Describe investigations into the requirements and products of photosynthesis.
Explain how chloroplasts are related to photosynthesis.
Explain enzyme action: active site, specificity and the lock and key model.
Explain the effects of substrate concentration, temperature and pH on enzyme-catalysed reactions.
Describe investigations into those effects.
Explain how temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect photosynthesis rate.
Describe investigations into environmental factors affecting photosynthesis.
Use the inverse square law to explain changes in rate with distance from a light source.
Explain how factors interact to limit photosynthesis, using graphs.
Calculate rates, plot graphs and interpret graphs, charts and tables for photosynthesis data.

topics.title: B3.2 How do producers get the substances they need?

outcomes.text: Describe the substances transported into and out of photosynthetic organisms.
Explain transport into and out of cells by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Describe investigations into diffusion and osmosis.
Explain how partially permeable membranes relate to diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Explain uptake of water and mineral ions, relating root hair cells to function.
Explain how xylem and phloem are adapted, and how to observe them with a microscope.
Describe transpiration and translocation, and the structure and function of stomata.
Describe how to use a simple potometer.
Explain how light intensity, air movement and temperature affect water uptake, and investigate it.
Calculate rates, plot graphs and calculate percentage mass gain and loss for water uptake.

topics.title: B3.3 How are organisms in an ecosystem interdependent?

outcomes.text: Explain the importance of sugars, fatty acids, glycerol and amino acids in building and breaking down carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
Describe qualitative tests for biological molecules.
Describe photosynthetic organisms as the main producers of food and biomass.
Describe substances, including dissolved food molecules, transported into organisms.
Describe levels of organisation from individual organism to whole ecosystem.
Explain the importance of interdependence and competition in a community.
Describe differences between trophic levels (separate science).
Describe pyramids of biomass and how biomass is lost between levels (separate science).
Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer between trophic levels (separate science).
Recall that substances such as carbon and water cycle through abiotic and biotic parts of an ecosystem.
Explain the importance of the carbon cycle and water cycle.
Explain the role of microorganisms in cycling substances.
Calculate percentages of mass in the use and cycling of substances.
Explain how temperature and water content affect decomposition rate in aerobic and anaerobic conditions (separate science).
Calculate rate changes in decay of biological material (separate science).

topics.title: B3.4 How are populations affected by conditions in an ecosystem?

outcomes.text: Explain how abiotic and biotic factors affect communities: conditions, toxic chemicals, resources, predators and pathogens.
Describe a field investigation of distribution and abundance and how to determine numbers in an area.
Calculate means, use fractions and percentages, and plot and interpret population data.

units.title: Chapter B4: Using food and controlling growth

topics.title: B4.1 What happens during cellular respiration?

outcomes.text: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration: conditions, inputs, outputs and ATP yields.
Explain why cellular respiration occurs continuously in all living cells.
Explain how mitochondria relate to cellular respiration.
Describe cellular respiration as an exothermic process.
Describe investigations into the effect of substrates on respiration rate in yeast.
Carry out rate calculations for respiration.

topics.title: B4.2 How do we know about mitochondria and other cell structures?

outcomes.text: Explain how electron microscopy increased understanding of sub-cellular structures.
Use number, size, scale and units for cells and sub-cellular structures.
Use estimation and calculate with numbers in standard form.

topics.title: B4.3 How do organisms grow and develop?

outcomes.text: Describe the cell cycle in growth, including interphase and mitosis, and how to observe mitosis.
Describe cancer as uncontrolled growth and division from changes in cells.
Explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes.
Describe the function of stem cells in embryonic and adult animals and meristems in plants.
Explain cell differentiation by switching genes on and off.

topics.title: B4.4 How is plant growth controlled? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Explain the role of plant hormones, including auxins in phototropism and gravitropism, and investigate auxin in phototropism.
Describe effects of gibberellins and ethene.
Describe ways people use plant hormones to control plant growth.

topics.title: B4.5 Should we use stem cells to treat damage and disease?

outcomes.text: Discuss benefits, risks and ethical issues of using stem cells in medicine.

units.title: Chapter B5: The human body - staying alive

topics.title: B5.1 How do substances get into, out of and around our bodies?

outcomes.text: Describe substances moved into and out of the body: oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, dissolved food and urea.
Explain how partially permeable animal cell membranes relate to diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Describe the circulatory system and its links with gaseous exchange, digestive and excretory systems.
Explain how the heart is adapted: cardiac muscle, chambers and valves.
Explain how arteries, veins and capillaries are adapted to their functions.
Explain how red blood cells and plasma are adapted to their functions.
Explain the need for exchange surfaces and a transport system in terms of surface area to volume ratio.
Calculate surface area to volume ratios.

topics.title: B5.2 How does the nervous system help us respond to changes?

outcomes.text: Explain how receptors, sensory neurons, the CNS, motor neurons and effectors work together.
Explain how nerve cells and synapses relate to their functions.
Explain the structure of a reflex arc, including the relay neuron, and describe investigations into reflexes.
Describe the brain's structure and the roles of cerebral cortex, cerebellum and brain stem (separate science).
Explain difficulties of investigating brain function, including fMRI and ethics (separate science).

topics.title: B5.3 How do hormones control responses in the human body?

outcomes.text: Describe the principles of hormonal coordination by the endocrine system.
Explain the roles of thyroxine, as a negative feedback example, and adrenaline.

topics.title: B5.4 Why do we need to maintain a constant internal environment?

outcomes.text: Explain the importance of a constant internal environment.
Describe the function of the skin in temperature control: sweating, hair erection and blood flow (separate science).
Explain the body's responses to temperature challenges, including negative feedback (separate science).
Explain the effect on cells of osmotic changes in body fluids.
Describe how the kidneys filter water and urea and maintain water balance (separate science).
Describe the effect of ADH on kidney tubule permeability (separate science).
Explain the body's response to osmotic challenges (separate science).
Extract, interpret and translate data in graphs, charts and tables.

topics.title: B5.5 What role do hormones play in human reproduction?

outcomes.text: Describe the role of hormones in human reproduction, including the menstrual cycle.
Explain the interactions of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone.
Explain hormonal contraception and evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods.
Explain the use of hormones in treating infertility.

topics.title: B5.6 What can happen when organs and control systems stop working?

outcomes.text: Explain how insulin controls blood sugar.
Explain how glucagon and insulin work together.
Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their treatment.

subtopics.title: The eye and nervous system damage

outcomes.text: Explain how eye structures relate to function, using ray diagrams: cornea, iris, lens, ciliary muscle and retina.
Describe investigations into pupil response to light (separate science).
Describe eye defects and how they are overcome, using ray diagrams (separate science).
Explain limitations in treating nervous system damage and the potential of stem cells (separate science).

units.title: Chapter B6: Life on Earth - past, present and future

topics.title: B6.1 How was the theory of evolution developed?

outcomes.text: State that populations usually show extensive genetic variation.
Recall that variants arise from mutations, most with no effect on phenotype.
Explain evolution through natural selection of variants suited to the environment.
Explain the importance of competition for natural selection.
Describe evolution as change in inherited characteristics over generations, possibly forming new species.
Explain the impact of selective breeding of food plants and domesticated animals.
Describe how fossils provide evidence for evolution.
Describe the work of Darwin and Wallace (separate science).
Describe modern evidence for evolution, such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
Explain the impact of these ideas on modern biology and society (separate science).

topics.title: B6.2 How do sexual and asexual reproduction affect evolution? (separate science only)

outcomes.text: Explain advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction in a range of organisms.

topics.title: B6.3 How does our understanding of biology help us classify the diversity of organisms on Earth?

outcomes.text: Describe the impact of developments in biology on classification, including DNA analysis.

topics.title: B6.4 How is biodiversity threatened and how can we protect it?

outcomes.text: Describe positive and negative human interactions within ecosystems and their impact on biodiversity.
Evaluate evidence for environmental change affecting distribution of organisms (separate science).
Describe biological factors affecting food security (separate science).
Explain benefits and challenges of maintaining local and global biodiversity.
Extract and interpret biodiversity data from charts, graphs and tables.
Describe biotechnological and agricultural solutions, including genetic modification, to feed a growing population (separate science).

topics.title: IaS1 What needs to be considered when investigating a phenomenon scientifically?

outcomes.text: Use scientific theories to develop and justify hypotheses and predictions.
Suggest apparatus, materials and techniques, justified by precision, accuracy and validity.
Recognise scientific quantities and how they are determined.
Identify factors to be controlled and how to control them.
Suggest and justify a sample size or range of values.
Plan clear, logically sequenced experiments or procedures.
Identify hazards and ways of minimising risk.
Use scientific vocabulary to communicate the rationale and methods of an investigation.

topics.title: IaS2 What conclusions can we make from data?

outcomes.text: Present observations and data in appropriate formats.
Use SI units, prefixes and powers of ten, and interconvert units.
Translate data between forms and use suitable significant figures.
Choose graph forms, scales and lines of best fit, and show uncertainty.
Identify patterns, use range and mean, and read gradients, interpolation and extrapolation from graphs.
Evaluate data for accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility, identify random and systematic error, and judge outliers.
Evaluate an experimental strategy, suggest improvements and further investigations.
Interpret data to make inferences and reasoned conclusions.
Explain how far data raise or lower confidence in a prediction or hypothesis.

topics.title: IaS3 How are scientific explanations developed?

outcomes.text: Identify correlations and distinguish correlation from cause-effect.
Suggest risk factors that increase the chance of an outcome without guaranteeing it.
Explain why individual cases are not convincing evidence, and why a plausible mechanism matters.
Describe examples of theories developing and being modified when new evidence arises.
Describe in outline the peer review process.
Use representational, spatial, descriptive, computational and mathematical models to solve problems, predict, explain and identify limits.

topics.title: IaS4 How do science and technology impact society?

outcomes.text: Describe and explain applications of science that made significant positive differences to lives.
Identify risks arising from new scientific or technological advances.
Identify risks and benefits for different groups, discuss courses of action, and distinguish perceived from calculated risk.
Suggest why different decisions on the same issue may suit different contexts and make evidence-based decisions.
Distinguish questions answerable by science from those that are not, and summarise differing views on ethical issues.
Explain why scientists should communicate their work to a range of audiences.
